hints: Look carefully at the diagram and find bond B first. It joins the top short chain down to the long bottom chain, so what type of bond must that branch be?
Now count the glucose units in the top short chain and check if bonds A and D are at the very end of a chain. Remember alpha-amylase only cuts internal 1,4 bonds in longer chains.
walkthrough:
**Recall the three rules for alpha-amylase**

Think of the enzyme as picky. It will only cut 1,4 bonds, never 1,6 branch bonds.

It also refuses to cut the last bond at the end of a chain, and it refuses to cut any bonds inside a tiny side chain of only three glucose units.

**Rule out the branch and the short side chain**

Bond B is the vertical link between the top chain and the bottom chain. That is the 1,6 branch point, so rule 1 says no.

The whole top row is a chain of exactly three glucose units attached by that 1,6 bond. Bond A is inside that three-unit chain, so rule 3 says no.

**Compare D and C in the long chain**

Bond D is at the far left end of the bottom chain. It is the last bond of a chain, so rule 2 says no.

Bond C is different. It is a 1,4 bond, it is in the middle of the long bottom chain (not the last bond), and it is not in a three-unit side chain. It passes all three rules, so it can be hydrolysed.

options.A: Bond A is a 1,4 bond but it lies inside the short three-glucose side chain, which alpha-amylase cannot hydrolyse.
options.B: Bond B is the 1,6 branch point joining the two chains, and alpha-amylase only hydrolyses 1,4 bonds.
options.C: Bond C is an internal 1,4 bond in the long main chain, not a last bond and not in a three-unit branch, so it can be hydrolysed.
options.D: Bond D is the last bond at the end of the bottom chain, which alpha-amylase is not able to hydrolyse.
